newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS-Swire gets perpetual.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS-Swire gets perpetual.

text.p: Asia saw its first perpetual bond on Thursday courtesy of Hong Kong's blue chip company Swire Pacific Ltd.

Asian debt markets also were busy with more traditional issues, with Associates Corp of North America launching one of the newly popular Euro-Asian issues and Bank of East Asia bringing a Hong Kong dollar issue.
Swire's US$300 million bond issue was launched Thursday morning via lead manager Merrill Lynch.
The bonds have a coupon of 9.33 percent and the issuer has the right to call them back from bondholders at par after 10 years and thereafter annually.
If the bonds are not called, they never mature.

Undated or perpetual debt ranks lower than senior debt on a Hong Kong company's balance sheet, but senior to equity. Consequently, the issue has been rated A-minus by Standard and Poor's Corp and Baa1 by Moody's Investors Service Inc. These ratings are one grade below Swire's senior debt ratings.

Merrill Lynch said that about 50 percent of the bond placed with investors in Asia, 10 percent in Europe and 40 percent in the U.S. The issue size was increased to US$300 million from US$150 million as a result of increased demand.
Most Asian bankers had expected the issue to place well in the U.S., where institutional investors are comfortable with long-term paper in general and are familiar with perpetuals.
The response in Asia, where most debt paper is short-dated and undated debt paper is mostly unknown, was more surprising.

"The issue might have gone into a few of the trading portfolios in some of the banks and to some of the fund managers, which would treat it as quasi equity," said a syndicate managers at a European bank here.
The high coupon and the Swire name would be the main attraction for Asian investors, bankers said.
"Anyone that knows the Swire group in the stock market would be interested," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
"And you are talking about a minimum return of 9.33 percent. I don't think that in the stock market you can actively speculate on that type of return," she said.
A Swire executive said raising funds with the perpetual bond is cheaper than issuing equity.
"In terms of our calculations, the cost of the perpetual bond is significantly less than equity, particularly after tax," said Martin Cubbon, finance manager at Swire Pacific.
Elsewhere, Lehman Brothers and Goldman Sachs brought a US$600 million five-year Euro-Asian bond for Associates Corp that was priced to yield 40 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Recently launched Euro-Asian bonds--which are listed on Asian and European exchanges--have found good demand in Asia.
About half of the 1.0 billion mark bond for Toyota Motor Credit Corp launched Wednesday by Merrill Lynch and SBC Warburg ended up in Asia. Swiss accounts also put in a good bid.
TMCC launched a dollar-denominated Euro-Asian deal last week that reportedly also found plenty of buyers in Asia.
Bank of East Asia's HK$1.8 billion three-year floating rate certificate of deposit issue was launched today through six arrangers.
Some bankers said that at 44 basis points all-in, the deal was priced too tightly versus Dah Sing Bank's HK$1.2 billion three-year FRCD launched Wednesday.
Dah Sing's deal pays 56 basis points all-in.
But others said Bank of East Asia should have no problem placing the paper. A company offical today said demand for the issue has been good and it could be raised to HK$2.5 billion.
In other news, Korea Development Bank has mandated Merrill Lynch and J.P. Morgan to arrange its next global bond.
